title: Ultragenyx ($RARE): A Catalyst-Driven Thesis With Asymmetric Upside
snippet: The first catalyst has already gone right. The second FDA decision and another pivotal readout create one of the most concentrated catalyst setups in biotech.
content_html:
After my previous successful investment in a small-to-mid cap biotech company Compass Pathways ( ), I decided to invest in another one. Here is my thesis. By the way, the CMPS position in My Private Portfolio is up over +42%.

Brief Introduction

Name: Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical Inc.
Ticker:
Sector: Healthcare
Industry: Biotechnology
Market Cap: $2.5 billion (small-to-mid-cap)
Date of Entry: 24 August 2026
Position Size: 1,000 shares
Average Price: $26.03

Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical isn’t your typical pre-revenue biotech company betting everything on one experimental drug and single binary FDA event, i.e. a lottery ticket. It already sells several rare-disease medicines, expects $730-760 million of revenue in 2026 and has now secured its 5th FDA approval.

However, as it usually goes with biotech companies at this stage, the company is still losing money, still burns substantial cash, and has given investors plenty of reasons to distrust it in the past. Most notably, its drug called ‘setrusumab’ failed the primary endpoints of two Phase 3 trials in December 2025, sending RARE down more than 40% in a single day. That happens with biotech…

So, is this a Hated Moat?

Ultragenyx got into the H2 of 2026 with 3 major catalysts packed into roughly 2 months. The first has already happened & gone right. O August 19, the FDA approved GENGLYCOS, the company’s first gene therapy. The second catalyst comes on September 19, when the FDA makes another decision on UX111 after rejecting the application last year largely over manufacturing deficiencies. The third one is the Phase 3 Aspire readout for GTX-102 in so-called Angelman syndrome, expected in September or October.

The interesting part - and one of the main reasons why I went it - is that the first mentioned catalyst substantially de-risked the second, yet the share price barely changed.

What Does The Company Do?

Ultragenyx is a US-based biotech company develops treatments for rare and ultra-rare genetic diseases affecting relatively few patients globally, but often with severe consequences and few or no existing treatments. Sometimes, we refer to these as “orphan drugs”.

That means it’s generally not trying to make the next cholesterol pill, sell it to 20 million people or become the next Novo Nordisk. It specifically and deliberately targets diseases affecting relatively small populations (i.e., sometimes literally only a few thousand commercially accessible patients worldwide), where there may be no existing treatment addressing the underlying disease.

Unlike many biotech companies, Ultragenyx is not pre-revenue. Before GENGLYCOS (the drug that FDA just approved), it already had 4 commercial products: Crysvita, Dojolvi, Evkeeza and Mepsevii. Don’t ask me who and how comes up with those names, but they’re still better than your regular monoclonal antibodies drug. Crysvita is by far the largest one, generating $156 million of Ultragenyx’s $214 million Q2 2026 revenue.

Its company’s moat is therefore more about the infrastructure built around rare diseases, not really about developing one miraculous product worth tens of billions in revenue. The moat is in identifying tiny patient populations, recruiting them into trials, navigating specialist treatment centres, gaining reimbursement for extremely expensive therapies, dealing with regulators, and then commercialising those drugs globally. One thing often omitted about “orphan drugs” is that they are generally in bigger favour to regulators than your typical block-buster drugs that are aimed to be sold in huge quantities. The emerging second layer for the company is gene-therapy manufacturing.

Ultragenyx spent heavily building its own facility in Bedford, Massachusetts. That initially looked more like a liability than a moat when FDA inspections contributed to the UX111 (a drug that we will talk about more) rejection in 2025. GENGLYCOS (the most recently approved drug by the FDA) changes the equation somewhat here. The FDA approval letter specifically authorises Ultragenyx’s Bedford facility to manufacture both the drug substance and final formulated product.

If the company can repeatedly push gene therapies through that same infrastructure, the enormous fixed investment starts becoming an advantage rather than an expense.

But this is biotech. A manufacturing moat cannot rescue a drug that doesn’t work. December’s setrusumab failure mentioned above, and the subsequent massive plummeting of the stock, is a good reminder of that.

Financials

Ultragenyx, despite growing, is, to put it plainly, nowhere near being profitable today. Revenue rose 20% in 2025 to $673 million. Q2 2026 revenue increased another 28% YoY to a record $214 million. Management currently guides to $730-760 million for 2026, representing roughly 8-13% growth. The important information here is that this guidance excludes revenue from new product launches such as the freshly approved GENGLYCOS (which is listed as a $2.7 million a pop!)

The ugly side of the biotech story is spending. Ultragenyx lost $92 million in Q2 and $277 million during the first six months of 2026. Operating cash burn reached $294 million in H1. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities fell from $737 million at year-end to $436 million by June 30. Management says that it’s enough to fund at least the next 12 months. To be honest, for a company with real revenue, this is not something I’d be particularly happy about. Causation, if anything.

There is no large conventional bank-debt balance, but the balance sheet isn’t really debt-free. Ultragenyx carries about $1.2 billion of liabilities tied to future Crysvita royalties that it previously sold to Royalty Pharma and OMERS. These aren’t ordinary bonds that suddenly mature and require repayment, but they represent future economics that no longer fully belong to shareholders.

The August approval helps here too. GENGLYCOS earned Ultragenyx a Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Voucher, which can be sold to another pharmaceutical company. A comparable voucher was sold by Rocket Pharmaceuticals for $180 million earlier this year. There is no guarantee Ultragenyx receives the same price, but this is potentially a meaningful source of non-dilutive capital for a company with $436 million of cash.

Management is simultaneously cutting costs and continues to target profitability in 2027. Whether it actually gets there will depend heavily on successful launches and pipeline execution but I’m definitely not underwriting 2027 profitability as a certainty and will remain rather sceptical and especially careful about the balance sheet, cash and its burn rate.

Investment Thesis

The easiest way to misunderstand this investment is to think “FDA approval in August = buy signal”. That’s not what happened in my case. :)

I believe the approval itself is less interesting than what it potentially tells us about what comes next.

Catalyst No. 1: GENGLYCOS (August 19, 2026)

GENGLYCOS (before known as DTX401) was approved on August 19. It was 4 days ahead of its August 23 FDA deadline. It became the first-ever FDA-approved treatment designed to address the underlying cause of glycogen storage disease type Ia and Ultragenyx’s first approved gene therapy ever. As mentioned above, the therapy was priced at $2.7 million (above expectations) and generated the Priority Review Voucher also discussed above.

Citi subsequently increased its target from $45 to $58, specifically noting that the $2.7 million price was about 33% above its assumption. Morgan Stanley moved from $67 to $74, JPMorgan from $75 to $80, Canaccord from $81 to $83 and Cantor from $96 to $103. I’m very vocal and reserved/sceptical about price targets of institution, especially in biotech where they can become obsolete overnight, but it shows you a pattern. Wall Street generally and virtually unanimously revised its assumptions upward while the stock itself did essentially nothing. And that was quite bizarre…

RARE closed at $26.24 on August 19. Immediately after the news in after hours, it popped +25%, and it got immediately absorbed to like overall +1%. Watching that price action was wild. The morning after approval it opened at $28.39 and touched $28.50, so a mild pop, and then spent the rest of the session collapsing to $25.32.

Did I hear “sell the news?”

By our August 24 entry it closed at $25.72 and as of August 28 it closed at $25.61.

In other words, the FDA approval, unexpectedly high pricing, PRV and first successful regulatory approval from the Bedford manufacturing operation have produced virtually no increase in the market value of the company whatsoever.

Some of that is rational. GSDIa is an ultra-rare disease, the commercial launch will take time, and investors know the much larger valuation swing comes from GTX-102 (Catalyst No. 3 discussed below).

Yet still, the drug was approved, the whole catalyst event went as smooth as possible, with multiple positives (which were even unexpected) announced and that deserved the pop in +10-20% area, surely. Instead, it got “sell the news” and the stock struggled to remain at least break-even? Well, fair enough I guess, but I still think the market underappreciated one piece of information.

Catalyst No. 2: UX111 (September 19, 2026)

UX111 is a one-time gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome Type A, a devastating childhood neurodegenerative disease with no approved treatment.

The FDA rejected the original application in July 2025 through what is formally called a Complete Response Letter (CRL), essentially meaning “we cannot approve this application in its current form.”

And this is one of the central points in my thesis. The CRL’s blocking deficiencies centred on CMC (i.e., chemistry, manufacturing and controls) and manufacturing-facility inspections. FDA inspectors back then said corrective actions were not yet comprehensive enough to resolve the observed issues and that additional verification could be required.

This means that the FDA didn’t say UX111 had failed clinically or identify an efficacy or safety deficiency. Ultragenyx later said the agency had described the neurodevelopmental data as robust and the biomarker evidence as supportive.

But to remain as unbiased as possible, it’s a fact that the actual CRL says the FDA was still evaluating whether the clinical evidence adequately supported the indication and requested updated safety, efficacy, MRI and biomarker data with the resubmission.

There was also another (small) stumble. Ultragenyx resubmitted UX111 early this year but received an Incomplete Response Letter in February, asking for additional documentation supporting its CMC responses. The package was subsequently completed, accepted for review on April 2, and assigned the new September 19, 2026 PDUFA date. So, will the third’s time be the charm?

and more importantly, why does GENGLYCOS matter here?

Well, it matters because Ultragenyx’s own filings said the UX111 CRL involved observations at its gene-therapy manufacturing facility and a third-party manufacturer. UX111 will use both Andelyn Biosciences and Ultragenyx’s Bedford operation. The FDA has now approved another gene therapy manufactured at Bedford.

That doesn’t mean UX111 is automatically approved. There are product-specific CMC questions and the Andelyn manufacturing component remains separate but one of the things that went visibly wrong last time (the Ultragenyx facility itself) now has an FDA-approved commercial gene therapy coming out of it.

The FDA event in August with GENGLYCOS being approved is basically an important regulatory win that de-risks UX111. If I should estimate for the sake of future accountability & possibility of being biblically wrong,I’d say there’s about 75% probability of UX111 getting approved and 25% probability of another delay or CRL.

Catalyst No. 3: GTX-102 (September/October 2026)

This is the big one and the most important one.

GTX-102, now called apazunersen (yeah, the names…), is an antisense therapy for Angelman syndrome, a serious neurodevelopmental disorder. The 48-week Phase 3 Aspire trial enrolled 129 children aged 4-17 and randomised them 1:1 between GTX-102 and a sham procedure. Unlike UX111, this isn’t principally a manufacturing bet. It’s the more traditional biotech-y one, a clinical-efficacy bet.

From the data I researched as a PhD in the field of medicine, the previous Phase 1/2 program is encouraging. 74 patients had been treated as of March, with average exposure exceeding 3 years and some patients approaching 5 years. The company reports continued developmental improvement and no new cases of the previously observed transient lower-extremity weakness. But those earlier data weren’t the same thing as a large randomised, sham-controlled Phase 3 study. Aspire now has to reproduce the signal properly and in the league of the “big boys”, as far as the scientific proof goes.

There is no fixed October date. Management says results should arrive in September or October. Wall Street remains divided here. Wells Fargo just increased its estimated probability of success from 60% to 75% and raised its target to $50. Guggenheim is more cautious but estimates that an overwhelmingly positive result could push RARE toward $55-65 per share, while outright failure could send it into the low teens. Morgan Stanley previously characterised the setup as roughly 50-70% upside on success versus approximately 20% downside on failure.

After doing some models and calculations, I’m using 60% probability of a clean positive readout, 15% mixed/ambiguous and 25% failure.

And this is where the most of the real upside (as well as most of the real risk) actually sits.

This results gives us a probability-weighted outcome of approximately $40.50, or roughly +56% from my $26.03 entry.

Be careful to note that that’s not “fair value.” It is an event tree built around what I think the stock could reasonably trade at after the 2 remaining catalysts.

For context, the current analyst average is around $55, but the range stretches from roughly $28 to $103. That spread tells us much more than the average does, and it’s ‘pathognomonic’ to biotech, i.e., nobody truly knows what RARE is worth until Aspire answers the most important remaining question.

My Plan

At $26.03 average, this is primarily a catalyst-driven swing position for me, not really a long-term position for years to come.

My first meaningful target is roughly $40 per share. If UX111 is approved on September 19 but the stock only moves into the high-$20s or low-$30s, I’m unlikely to sell simply because the event has passed. The bigger catalyst remains the latter one, Aspire.

If UX111 approval pushes RARE toward $35-40 before the Angelman data, the equation of this trade changes. I believe that at that point the market will already be pricing in substantially more optimism, and in usch case, I’d likely trim roughly 25-50% of the position rather than carry the entire investment through a high-risk binary set-up of Phase 3 readout.

Above $40 before Aspire, I’m gonna de-risk even more aggressively. If UX111 receives another CRL, I’ll read that letter before doing anything, despite almost surely being down in a hole called “double-digit”. Another narrow, fixable CMC issue is frustrating but doesn’t necessarily destroy the investment thesis with Aspire immediately ahead. A little bagholding never killed nobody. A newly identified efficacy or safety problem, though, would be fundamentally different and would likely force me to reduce the position or exit it entirely.

If Aspire is unequivocally positive and everything goes as smoothly as the August event, my mindset changes from swing trade to potential longer-term investment. With GENGLYCOS approved, UX111 potentially approved, GTX-102 clinically validated and the existing commercial portfolio still growing, the business would look materially different from the one currently valued at roughly $2.5 billion. In that scenario, $50-60 becomes a reasonable first longer-term valuation range, an I’d be comfortable retaining a core position into the launches and the attempted transition toward profitability in 2027.

A mixed Aspire result needs to be treated as, well, mixed. A technically significant secondary endpoint without convincing clinical breadth isn’t automatically bullish just because management can call the trial “statistically successful.” And if Aspire simply fails, I don’t think there’s much justification for bagholding. The losses will be most likely cut in such scenario.

I’m willing to hold an underwater position when price has changed but the thesis has not but I‘m not willing to hold one when the reason I bought for has disappeared. If UX111 suffers a meaningful regulatory failure and Aspire fails, this thesis is broken, I’ll take the L and move on.

Final Thoughts

The reason I own RARE today is truly simple. 1 of 3 major events has already gone right this month (August 2026), that event appears to have improved the odds of the second one going right as well, and the market has given the company almost no lasting credit for either the approval itself or that read-through.

While not quite sure about ‘Hated’ Moat in this case, it surely does feel like an ‘Underappreciated’ Moat. :) A ‘I’m not impressed’ show-me phase type of a moat with potentially great upside, though with a big risk embedded as well. That’s why the position sizing is everything in investments like these.

At $26, I believe it’s worth the risk.
